body: Arguably this function is parsing ASCII and has undefined behavior for extended characters (`latin1`). I hope somebody with more knowledge of encodings can weigh in on what this function actually does and should be called like.

I would not call this one parse, that's just a simple memcpy, no interpretation of the underlying format. I fyou really want the parse prefix, then probably ASCII then, there is higher chance that people will find it than latin 1.

There is definitely an interpretation going on. If nothing else, it's "utf-32 but only the first 255 values". Though that's not what it's used like. More often than not, it's used to construct strings from c strings, which from a cursory search is partially undefined behavior? Not exactly something you want to "just copy from".

I did some more digging. Apparently C strings are encoded by whatever `-fexec-charset` (GCC / Clang) or `/execution-charset` (MSVC) is set to. MSVC defaults to 'system locale encodings' while GCC / clang default to UTF-8. In the codebase, `/utf-8` is used to set MSVC to UTF-8 as well. In any case, whatever we're doing with these strings by passing them into _this_ function is wrong, and only doesn't cause problems because of low-bit overlaps of the encodings...

> Arguably this function is parsing ASCII and has undefined behavior for extended characters (latin1).

What's undefined? Every defined Latin-1 (ISO-8859-1) character correspond one-to-one to the same character in the Unicode Basic Latin and Latin-1 Supplement blocks.

> /execution-charset (MSVC) is set to

It's already set to UTF-8: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/b9437c393871c377b5ece131afaf831e78dfb6f8/platform/windows/detect.py#L443

Yes, I found this statement now too. Turns out we've been parsing `UTF-8` encoded string literals incorrectly using an ascii parsing function this whole time. The main reason we haven't run into trouble is because they overlap until 127, and nobody's used non-ascii characters in a string literal yet....

I've settled for renaming it to `parse_ascii` and failing for values above 127. The only other correct choices would be
- to call it `ascii_unchecked` and not to bother checking for values above 127, as is the case now
- to use the `parse_utf8` function for the `String` constructor instead, but that would come with unnecessary slow-downs, since we aren't using UTF-8 string literals (so far) anyway.

> Turns out we've been parsing UTF-8 encoded string literals incorrectly using an ascii parsing function this whole time.

I think it was a deliberate choice to avoid unnecessary parsing, string literals in the code are either ASCII or `U".."` literals when it's necessary.

> The main reason we haven't run into trouble is because they overlap until 127, and nobody's used non-ascii characters in a string literal yet....

This happened few times.

Also, it is documented to be Latin-1 in the GDExtension interface, so changing it to only handle ASCII (which is fine for the engine code) is a breaking change:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/b9437c393871c377b5ece131afaf831e78dfb6f8/core/extension/gdextension_interface.h#L1584-L1593

Ok, fine with me — so we don't change any behavior and call the function `parse_latin1`? This is what I had originally. 
It would still be incorrect for utf-8 string literals, which should probably get a dedicated `ascii` function in a follow-up PR.

I guess we can have both `ascii` (to use with literals) and `latin-1` (for GDExtensions).
Or keep `latin-1` for GDExtensions (for compatibility and mark it as deprecated) and only use `parse_utf8` for literals (probably better).

If the script can specify its latin1, then yeah, `parse_latin1` makes a lot of sense. But you are right, a dedicated ascii one for in engine seems better, to avoid some silent errors. Maybe even switch to `parse_utf8` for those, as static string are generally pretty small, should not be too much cycles wasted (and we have a [PR](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/99826) to speed that up (shameless plug))

I think an `ascii` function would be good to have as it would be the fastest way to parse string literals correctly, especially since almost all of them are unlikely to use non-ascii characters anyway. If we want to enforce this, it may be possible to do it with `-fexec-charset` and the corresponding MSVC function.

I _could_ add an `ascii` function in this PR, but I think it's out of scope. I think it's better to call the existing function `latin` and call it a day, and try to address the implications of the mismatch in a follow-up PR. Especially since just switching the default would, as @bruvzg pointed out, technically be a breaking change.

I'm not sure we really need the `ascii` one though. The only error right now is interpreting utf8 as latin1 for static strings. So we should use `parse_utf8` there, but I don't know what would be the use of an `ascii` one that would not be covered by `latin1` ( or maybe I'm just not seeing it)

Its use-case would be that it would be faster than `parse_utf8()`, but unlike `parse_latin1()` it would not be incorrect for string literals, instead logging an error on values > 127. So it could be safely used for most string literals.

Oh ok, I see. Well I would be in favor of being always correct and always use `parse_utf8`. If we define it as utf-8 in the compilation toolchain, then stick to it and parse utf8. This will probably not even make a noticable speed difference, and if it did, then we can go speed it up again. But correctness seems more important than performance here.
Let's discuss this in follow-up PRs. I think we can agree that the current implementation parses `latin1`, which should be enough to finish up this PR.
Leftover? How it is related to this PR?
